lessons.title: Asymptotes and curve sketching
lessons.summary: Build a sketch from the domain, polynomial division and one-sided limits.
lessons.objective: Identify genuine asymptotes and combine exact features into a consistent sketch.
lessons.before: You need polynomial division, factorisation and differentiation. Review roots and coefficients when finding intercepts.
lessons.ideas:
A rational function is a quotient \(f(x)=P(x)/Q(x)\) of polynomials. Start with \(Q(x)\ne0\). A cancelled factor leaves a missing input in the original domain.

Poles and missing points

If \(Q(h)=0\) and \(P(h)\ne0\), the graph has a vertical asymptote \(x=h\). Determine the sign of the unbounded value separately on each side. If factors cancel, inspect the remaining expression: cancellation may leave a finite hole instead.

What happens far away?

Write \(P=QS+R\), with \(\deg R<\deg Q\). Then

\[f(x)=S(x)+\frac{R(x)}{Q(x)}.\]

The final term tends to zero. A constant \(S\) gives a horizontal asymptote; a linear \(S=mx+c\) gives an oblique asymptote. A higher-degree quotient is not a straight-line asymptote. When \(\deg P<\deg Q\), the horizontal asymptote is \(y=0\).

A sketch is a collection of checked facts

Find admissible zeros of \(P\), the value at \(x=0\) when defined, and the stationary points. A horizontal asymptote can be crossed: solve \(f(x)=c\) rather than treating the height \(c\) as forbidden. Never join branches across an excluded input.
lessons.method:
1. Record the original domain and factor both polynomials.
  2. Divide to identify the asymptote at infinity.
  3. Calculate intercepts, stationary points and one-sided limits.
  4. Draw separate branches, label exact coordinates and check their directions.
mistakes: A denominator zero is not automatically a vertical asymptote after cancellation.
An asymptote describes limiting behaviour; it does not forbid a crossing.
An open circle must retain the excluded input even when the simplified expression is a line.
A sketch must show the sign of each approach to a pole, not just a dashed line.

examples.title: 1 · Division reveals the branches
examples.question: Find the asymptotes and axis intersections of \(f(x)=\frac{2x^2-3x+4}{x+2}\).
examples.solution:
\[f(x)=2x-7+\frac{18}{x+2}.\]

The domain excludes \(-2\); the numerator there is \(18\), so \(x=-2\) is a vertical asymptote. The oblique asymptote is \(y=2x-7\). As \(x\to-2^-\), \(f(x)\to-\infty\); from the right it tends to \(+\infty\). The numerator has discriminant \(9-32=-23\), so there are no real x-intercepts. The y-intercept is \((0,2)\).

examples.title: 2 · A hole is different from a pole
examples.question: Describe the graph of \(f(x)=\frac{x^2-x-6}{x-3}\).
examples.solution:
\[x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2).\]

Thus \(f(x)=x+2\) for \(x\ne3\). Draw the line with an open circle at \((3,5)\). There is no vertical asymptote at \(3\): the limit is \(5\), not infinity. The original expression still has no value at that input.

examples.title: 3 · Crossing a horizontal asymptote
examples.question: Find the horizontal asymptote of \(f(x)=\frac{3x^2+x+5}{x^2+1}\), and determine whether the graph crosses it.
examples.solution:
\[f(x)=3+\frac{x+2}{x^2+1}.\]

The denominator is positive for every real input. The remainder tends to zero, so the asymptote is \(y=3\). Setting \(f(x)=3\) gives \(x+2=0\), hence the crossing is \((-2,3)\). The sign of \(x+2\) changes there, so this is a crossing rather than just a contact.

examples.title: 4 · Complete the branch information
examples.question: Find and classify the stationary points of \(f(x)=\frac{x^2-4x+7}{x-2}\), and state its asymptotes.
examples.solution:
\[f(x)=x-2+\frac3{x-2},\qquad f^\prime(x)=1-\frac3{(x-2)^2}.\]

The asymptotes are \(x=2\) and \(y=x-2\). The stationary inputs are \(2\pm\sqrt3\), giving points \((2-\sqrt3,-2\sqrt3)\) and \((2+\sqrt3,2\sqrt3)\). The derivative changes from positive to negative at the left point (maximum), and from negative to positive at the right point (minimum). Each branch stays on its own side of the vertical asymptote.

lessons.title: Ranges and stationary points
lessons.summary: Find attained heights and distinguish an endpoint from an unattained limit.
lessons.objective: Use discriminants, derivatives and domain checks to give the complete exact range.
lessons.ideas:
The range is the set of output values actually attained by an allowed input. A limiting height need not belong to the range, and a horizontal asymptote is not automatically excluded.

Turn an output into an existence question

Set \(y=P(x)/Q(x)\) and rearrange to \(yQ(x)-P(x)=0\), keeping \(Q(x)\ne0\). If the equation is quadratic in \(x\), real candidates require a non-negative discriminant. Check values of \(y\) for which the quadratic coefficient vanishes separately: the equation may become linear, contradictory or identically true.

Stationary points and boundaries

A zero of \(f^\prime\) is relevant only within the domain. A sign change from \(+\) to \(-\) gives a local maximum; the reverse gives a local minimum. On a restricted domain, inspect its endpoints and limiting values too. Include an output endpoint only when some permitted input attains it.

Check every candidate input

A discriminant calculation creates candidates, not permission to use a pole or a cancelled input. Substitute back into the original domain. An excluded input can remove an otherwise attainable-looking height.
lessons.method:
1. State the domain and write an equation for a general output \(y\).
  2. Use its discriminant or an exact inequality to find candidate heights.
  3. Check degenerate equations, poles and restricted endpoints.
  4. Give a complete set of heights with correct open or closed boundaries.
mistakes: The sign of the derivative alone does not decide whether an endpoint is attained.
Do not divide by the leading coefficient in the output equation before checking when it is zero.
A range contains y-values, not the x-coordinates of stationary points.
The original domain remains in force after clearing denominators.

examples.title: 1 · A gap in the range
examples.question: Find the exact range of \(f(x)=x+\frac9x\), for \(x\ne0\).
examples.solution:
\[x^2-yx+9=0,\qquad \Delta=y^2-36.\]

A real input exists precisely when \(y\le-6\) or \(y\ge6\). No candidate input can be \(0\), since the constant term is \(9\). The endpoints are attained at \(x=-3\) and \(x=3\). Thus the range is \((-\infty,-6]\cup[6,\infty)\).

examples.title: 2 · A limit which is never reached
examples.question: Find the range of \(f(x)=\frac{2x^2+7}{x^2+1}\).
examples.solution:
\[f(x)=2+\frac5{x^2+1}.\]

Since \(x^2+1\ge1\), the fraction is positive and at most \(5\). Its largest value is attained at \(x=0\), but it is never zero. The range is therefore \((2,7]\). The asymptote \(y=2\) is excluded here because the remainder cannot vanish.

examples.title: 3 · Do not lose the linear case
examples.question: Find the range of \(f(x)=\frac{x^2+2x+2}{x^2+1}\) using a discriminant.
examples.solution:
\[(y-1)x^2-2x+(y-2)=0.\]

For \(y\ne1\), the discriminant condition is

\[4-4(y-1)(y-2)\ge0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y^2-3y+1\le0.\]

The boundary values are \((3-\sqrt5)/2\) and \((3+\sqrt5)/2\). At \(y=1\), the equation becomes \(-2x-1=0\), which has the allowed input \(-1/2\). The denominator is always positive, and both boundary values are attained. The full range is \(\left[\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2},\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\right]\).

examples.title: 4 · An open input boundary changes the range
examples.question: Find the range of \(f(x)=x+\frac4x\) on \(0<x<2\).
examples.solution:
\[f^\prime(x)=1-\frac4{x^2}<0\qquad(0<x<2).\]

The function is continuous and strictly decreasing on this domain. It tends to \(+\infty\) as \(x\to0^+\), and to \(4\) as \(x\to2^-\). The input \(2\) is excluded and there is no other input in this interval giving \(4\). Hence the range is \((4,\infty)\).

lessons.title: Parameter families and reconstruction
lessons.summary: Recover coefficients and identify the exceptional members of a family.
lessons.objective: Translate graph features into coefficient equations without losing cancellation cases.
lessons.ideas:
A useful form for a quadratic numerator over a linear denominator is

\[f(x)=mx+c+\frac{R}{x-h},\qquad x\ne h.\]

Expanding \((mx+c)(x-h)+R\) reconstructs the numerator. A given point supplies another equation; a stationary input supplies \(f^\prime(x)=0\).

Parameters can change the graph type

If \(R=0\), the apparent pole becomes a missing point on a line. This exceptional case must be considered before claiming a vertical asymptote. If \(m>0\),

\[f^\prime(x)=m-\frac{R}{(x-h)^2}.\]

There are two stationary inputs when \(R>0\), and none when \(R\le0\). At \(R=0\), the domain still excludes \(h\).

Reconstruction and tangency

A double numerator root can give tangency to the x-axis only if the denominator is non-zero there. A numerator zero at a cancelled pole does not give a point of contact. Check that reconstructed coefficients satisfy all the original features, including a genuine pole.
lessons.method:
1. Write an identity based on the asymptote or factorisation.
  2. Use points, zeros or stationary inputs to solve for the remaining parameters.
  3. Separate zero remainders and vanishing coefficients.
  4. Verify each condition in the original rational function and classify the resulting branches.
mistakes: Matching an oblique asymptote gives two coefficient conditions, not the whole numerator.
An excluded input cannot be a stationary point or an intercept.
Include the equality case when a parameter makes the derivative constant.
A positive discriminant is not enough if a candidate lies at a pole.

examples.title: 1 · Reconstruct from asymptotes and a point
examples.question: The curve \(f(x)=\frac{ax^2+bx+c}{x-1}\) has oblique asymptote \(y=2x+5\) and passes through \((0,-3)\). Find \(a,b,c\).
examples.solution:
\[ax^2+bx+c=(2x+5)(x-1)+R=2x^2+3x+(R-5).\]

Thus \(a=2\), \(b=3\). At \(x=0\), \(f(0)=-c=-3\), so \(c=3\) and \(R=8\). The non-zero remainder confirms the vertical asymptote \(x=1\).

examples.title: 2 · A family with an exceptional line
examples.question: For \(f_k(x)=\frac{x^2+k}{x-2}\), find all \(k\) for which there are no stationary points. Describe the exceptional graph.
examples.solution:
\[f_k(x)=x+2+\frac{k+4}{x-2},\qquad f_k^\prime(x)=1-\frac{k+4}{(x-2)^2}.\]

If \(k+4>0\), there are two stationary inputs. If \(k+4\le0\), the derivative is positive everywhere in the domain, so the answer is \(k\le-4\). At \(k=-4\), the graph is the line \(y=x+2\) with a hole at \((2,4)\); the missing input remains excluded.

examples.title: 3 · Use a repeated intercept
examples.question: The curve \(f(x)=\frac{x^2+bx+c}{x+1}\) touches the x-axis at \(x=2\). Find \(b,c\) and check that the point is on the curve.
examples.solution:
Touching the x-axis requires a repeated numerator root, so

\[x^2+bx+c=(x-2)^2=x^2-4x+4.\]

Hence \(b=-4\), \(c=4\). The denominator at \(2\) is \(3\), so \((2,0)\) is permitted. Locally \(f(x)\ge0\), confirming tangency rather than a crossing.

examples.title: 4 · A stationary input fixes a remainder
examples.question: A curve has form \(f(x)=x+1+\frac{A}{x+2}\) and a stationary point at \(x=1\). Determine \(A\) and both stationary points.
examples.solution:
\[f^\prime(x)=1-\frac{A}{(x+2)^2}.\]

At \(1\), the derivative is zero, so \(A=9\). The stationary equation is \((x+2)^2=9\), giving \(x=-5,1\). Substitution gives \((-5,-7)\) and \((1,5)\). The derivative changes \(+\to-\) at the first (maximum) and \(-\to+\) at the second (minimum).

lessons.title: Modulus and inequalities
lessons.summary: Keep poles separate from equality boundaries in a complete sign analysis.
lessons.objective: Solve rational and modulus inequalities with every endpoint and domain restriction checked.
lessons.before: Review domains and branch signs and quadratic inequalities.
lessons.ideas:
Multiplying an inequality by an expression of unknown sign can reverse it. Use a sign chart, or multiply by a square known to be positive on the domain, retaining the excluded inputs.

Modulus of an output

The graph \(y=|f(x)|\) keeps the non-negative portions and reflects negative portions in the x-axis. For \(c>0\),

\[|f(x)|<c\iff -c<f(x)<c.\]

Equivalently, square both sides when both sides are non-negative. The squared inequality still excludes every original pole. For \(\le\), include valid equality inputs; a pole is never an equality input.

Modulus of an input

The graph \(y=f(|x|)\) uses the original right-hand half, reflected in the y-axis. Set \(u=|x|\ge0\), solve for \(u\), then reflect the allowed set. This is different from reflecting negative outputs. A cusp at \(0\) is possible; if \(f^\prime(0)=0\), inspect the local expression before calling it a corner.

Read the literal inequality

An auxiliary rational graph may have poles even when the actual inequality contains no division. Decide its domain from the stated inequality. For example, comparing two absolute polynomial expressions does not introduce excluded inputs.
lessons.method:
1. State the domain of the actual expression.
  2. Find all zero boundaries and poles; order them exactly.
  3. Test the sign on each interval, or use an equivalent non-negative square comparison.
  4. Include allowed equality boundaries for non-strict inequalities and give the whole union.
mistakes: Do not multiply by a denominator without considering its sign.
An auxiliary pole need not be excluded from an inequality which originally has no denominator.
Reflecting the right-hand half describes \(f(|x|)\); it does not describe \(|f(x)|\).
Keep strict endpoints open and never include a genuine pole.

examples.title: 1 · A sign chart with an included zero
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{x-2}{x+1}\ge0\).
examples.solution:
The critical inputs are \(-1\) (excluded) and \(2\) (a zero). The signs on the three intervals are \(+,-,+\). The zero at \(2\) is allowed because the inequality is non-strict. Thus

\[x\in(-\infty,-1)\cup[2,\infty).\]

examples.title: 2 · Square only after recording the domain
examples.question: Solve \(\left|\frac{x-1}{x+2}\right|<2\).
examples.solution:
First exclude \(x=-2\). Since both sides are non-negative, squaring is equivalent:

\[(x-1)^2<4(x+2)^2\iff3(x+1)(x+5)>0.\]

The solution is \((-\infty,-5)\cup(-1,\infty)\). The original pole already lies outside this set; it must still be checked explicitly.

examples.title: 3 · Reflect an input solution set
examples.question: For \(f(u)=\frac{u+1}{u-3}\), solve \(f(|x|)\le-1\).
examples.solution:
Put \(u=|x|\ge0\), with \(u\ne3\). Then

\[\frac{u+1}{u-3}+1=\frac{2(u-1)}{u-3}\le0.\]

The allowed non-negative inputs are \(1\le u<3\). Reflecting this interval gives

\[x\in(-3,-1]\cup[1,3).\]

examples.title: 4 · Do not invent a domain restriction
examples.question: Solve the literal inequality \(|x+2|\ge|x-1|\).
examples.solution:
Both sides are defined for every real \(x\). Squaring gives

\[(x+2)^2-(x-1)^2=6x+3\ge0.\]

Thus \(x\ge-1/2\). If a quotient were used to compare the two sides, its extra excluded inputs would have to be checked separately; the original inequality includes \(x=1\).

lessons.title: Relationships between curves
lessons.summary: Compare related curves without discarding inherited holes or sign cases.
lessons.objective: Determine domains, real branches and exact comparison sets for related rational curves.
lessons.before: Use rational sign charts and range and endpoint checks.
lessons.ideas:
A reciprocal keeps the original restrictions

If \(g=1/f\) is defined from an existing function, its domain is the domain of \(f\) with all zeros of \(f\) removed. Simplifying \(1/f\) does not fill the original holes. Non-zero stationary values map from \(y\) to \(1/y\), since

\[g^\prime(x)=-\frac{f^\prime(x)}{f(x)^2}.\]

A square-root relation has two branches

The relation \(y^2=f(x)\) has real points only where \(f(x)\ge0\). It contains both \(y=\sqrt{f(x)}\) and \(y=-\sqrt{f(x)}\), meeting where \(f=0\). An isolated admissible input can give an isolated real point. This relation is different from \(y=|f(x)|\).

Compare by subtracting

To decide which curve is higher, study \(g-f\) on their common domain. For a reciprocal comparison,

\[\frac1{f(x)}-f(x)=\frac{1-f(x)^2}{f(x)}.\]

The sign of \(f\) matters. Multiplying by \(f\) without a sign split loses valid intervals. Locate every zero boundary and pole of the difference before combining the solution set.
lessons.method:
1. Find the common domain, including inherited exclusions.
  2. Translate intercepts and stationary values only at valid inputs.
  3. Subtract the expressions or determine where the square-root relation is real.
  4. Check equality and exceptional inputs, then give all branches or intervals.
mistakes: A simplified reciprocal may have a zero at an input which was excluded originally.
The equation \(y^2=f(x)\) has two real branches where \(f(x)>0\).
An isolated zero of \(f\) can survive as an isolated point of the relation.
A reciprocal inequality cannot be multiplied by \(f(x)\) without knowing its sign.

examples.title: 1 · A reciprocal with an inherited hole
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\frac{x-1}{x+2}\) on its natural domain and define \(g=1/f\). State the domain and graph features of \(g\).
examples.solution:
\[g(x)=\frac{x+2}{x-1},\qquad x\notin\{-2,1\}.\]

The input \(-2\) remains excluded from the definition of \(f\), while \(1\) is excluded because \(f(1)=0\). The graph has a vertical asymptote \(x=1\), horizontal asymptote \(y=1\), and an open circle at \((-2,0)\). That open circle is not an x-intercept.

examples.title: 2 · A relation is not a single function
examples.question: Find the real x-domain and branches of \(y^2=\frac{x-1}{x+2}\).
examples.solution:
The quotient must be non-negative and its denominator non-zero. Its sign chart gives

\[x\in(-\infty,-2)\cup[1,\infty).\]

For interior inputs both \(y=\sqrt{(x-1)/(x+2)}\) and its negative occur. They meet at \((1,0)\). No real points exist for \(-2<x<1\), and \(x=-2\) is excluded.

examples.title: 3 · Compare a function with its reciprocal
examples.question: For \(f(x)=\frac{x-2}{x+1}\), solve \(1/f(x)>f(x)\).
examples.solution:
The common domain excludes \(-1\) and \(2\). Subtract without multiplying by an unknown sign:

\[\frac1f-f=\frac{(x+1)^2-(x-2)^2}{(x-2)(x+1)}=\frac{3(2x-1)}{(x-2)(x+1)}.\]

The critical inputs are \(-1,1/2,2\). The positive intervals give

\[x\in(-1,1/2)\cup(2,\infty).\]

The equality input \(1/2\) is excluded because the comparison is strict.

examples.title: 4 · Shared asymptotes do not force intersections
examples.question: Compare \(f(x)=x+5+\frac4{x-1}\) and \(g(x)=x+5+\frac9{x-1}\).
examples.solution:
\[g(x)-f(x)=\frac5{x-1}.\]

The curves share \(x=1\) and \(y=x+5\) as asymptotes. The difference is never zero, so they do not intersect. For \(x<1\), \(g\) is below \(f\); for \(x>1\), \(g\) is above \(f\). The common pole is excluded from both curves.

questions.title: A horizontal asymptote that the curve crosses
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{3 x^{2} - 8 x + 16}{x^{2} - x - 2}\]

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. Express \(f(x)\) in the form \(3+\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{B}{x+1}\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact coordinates of all stationary points and identify their nature.

    [4]

  3. Determine every straight-line asymptote of \(C\).

    [3]

  4. Sketch \(C\), labelling the asymptotes and all intersections with the coordinate axes.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(A=4,\ B=-9\).

(b) \(\left(\frac{4}{5},- \frac{16}{3}\right)\) (maximum); \(\left(8,\frac{8}{3}\right)\) (minimum).

(c) \(x=-1,\quad x=2,\quad y=3\)

(d) Sketch with the stated asymptotes, correct one-sided approaches and all intercepts.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Subtract 3 and equate the remaining numerators:

\[-5x+22=A(x+1)+B(x-2)\]

Hence \(A+B=-5\) and \(A-2B=22\), giving \(A=4,\ B=-9\).

(b)

Differentiating and simplifying gives

\[f'(x)=\frac{\left(x - 8\right) \left(5 x - 4\right)}{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} \left(x + 1\right)^{2}}\]

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[\left(x - 8\right) \left(5 x - 4\right)=0\]

The admissible solutions are \(x=\frac{4}{5},\quad x=8\). Substitution into \(f\) gives:

  • \(\left(\frac{4}{5},- \frac{16}{3}\right)\) — local maximum.
  • \(\left(8,\frac{8}{3}\right)\) — local minimum.

The classifications follow from the sign change of \(f'(x)\) (or the sign of \(f''(x)\)) at each point.

(c)

Polynomial division gives

\[f(x)=\frac{22 - 5 x}{x^{2} - x - 2} + 3\]

The numerator is non-zero at each real denominator zero. These are genuine vertical asymptotes: \(x=-1,\quad x=2\).

The remainder term tends to zero as \(x\to\pm\infty\). Hence the horizontal asymptote is \(y=3\).

(d)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=-1,\quad x=2,\quad y=3\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are absent: the numerator has no admissible real zeros.

At \(x=0\), \(y=-8\), giving \(\left(0,-8\right)\).

The curve meets its horizontal asymptote at \(\left(\frac{22}{5},3\right)\). This crossing is allowed; an asymptote need not be an unattained height.

\[x\to -1^-:\ y\to \infty,\qquad x\to -1^+:\ y\to -\infty\]
\[x\to 2^-:\ y\to -\infty,\qquad x\to 2^+:\ y\to \infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.
questions.hint_html: Subtract the limiting height first. Partial fractions then simplify both the derivative and the horizontal-asymptote crossing.

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[2 \left(x^{2} + 4 x + 2\right)=0\]

questions.title: When a supposed asymptote becomes a hole
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{\lambda + x^{2} - 6 x}{x - 1}\]

\(\lambda\in\mathbb R\). The domain always excludes \(x=1\).

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. Identify the exceptional value of \(\lambda\) for which \(x=1\) is not a vertical asymptote, and describe that graph. State the asymptotes in all other cases.

    [3]

  2. Find the value of \(\lambda\) for which the x-axis is tangent to the curve, and sketch that member.

    [4]

  3. Sketch the member with \(\lambda=4\), giving its exact axis intersections.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\lambda=5\) gives a punctured line; otherwise \(x=1,\ y=x-5\).

(b) \(\lambda=9\); tangency at \((3,0)\).

(c) Sketch with the stated asymptotes, correct one-sided approaches and all intercepts.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For every \(\lambda\), division gives

\[f(x)=x-5+\frac{\lambda-5}{x-1}\]

If \(\lambda\ne5\), the vertical asymptote is \(x=1\) and the oblique asymptote is \(y=x-5\). If \(\lambda=5\), the function is the line \(y=x-5\) with the point \((1,-4)\) removed. There is no vertical asymptote in that case.

(b)

A tangency to the x-axis requires a repeated numerator zero in the domain:

\[(-6)^2-4\lambda=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\lambda=9\]

Then \(f(x)=(x-3)^2/(x-1)\) touches the axis at \((3,0)\).

Differentiating and simplifying gives

\[f'(x)=\frac{\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 1\right)}{\left(x - 1\right)^{2}}\]

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 1\right)=0\]

The admissible solutions are \(x=-1,\quad x=3\). Substitution into \(f\) gives:

  • \(\left(-1,-8\right)\) — local maximum.
  • \(\left(3,0\right)\) — local minimum.

The classifications follow from the sign change of \(f'(x)\) (or the sign of \(f''(x)\)) at each point.

(c)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=1,\quad y=x - 5\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are \(\left(3 - \sqrt{5},0\right),\quad \left(\sqrt{5} + 3,0\right)\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=-4\), giving \(\left(0,-4\right)\).

\[x\to 1^-:\ y\to \infty,\qquad x\to 1^+:\ y\to -\infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

questions.title: Reconstruction from a turning-point input
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{a x^{2} + b x + c}{d + x}\]

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. The curve has asymptotes \(x=3\) and \(y=x-4\). One stationary point has x-coordinate 5. Determine \(a,b,c,d\).

    [5]

  2. Determine the exact range of \(f\), using an equation in \(x\) and a discriminant. Justify every included or excluded endpoint.

    [4]

  3. Sketch the reconstructed curve, indicating its turning points and intercepts.

    [3]

  4. Find all heights \(h\) for which \(f(x)=h\) has exactly one real solution.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(a=1,\ b=-7,\ c=16,\ d=-3\)

(b) \(y\in \left(-\infty, -5\right] \cup \left[3, \infty\right)\).

(c) Sketch with the stated asymptotes, correct one-sided approaches and all intercepts.

(d) \(h\in\{-5,3\}\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The vertical asymptote gives \(d=-3\). The oblique asymptote fixes the quotient as \(x-4\), so write

\[f(x)=x-4+\frac{R}{x-3}\]

At the stationary input \(x=5\), \(1-R/(5-3)^2=0\), so \(R=4\). Expanding \((x-3)(x-4)+4\) gives \(x^2-7x+16\).

(b)

Treat the curve equation as an equation for a real \(x\) at a prescribed height \(y\):

\[- x^{2} + x \left(y + 7\right) - 3 y - 16=0\]

When the quadratic coefficient is non-zero, real roots require

\[\Delta=\left(y - 3\right) \left(y + 5\right)\ge0\]

Solving this inequality gives the possible height intervals. Values at which the quadratic coefficient vanishes must be checked in the original equation.

No root of this equation can be a pole, because the numerator and denominator have no common zero. The attainable endpoint heights are included. Therefore the exact range is

\[y\in \left(-\infty, -5\right] \cup \left[3, \infty\right)\]

(c)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=3,\quad y=x - 4\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are absent: the numerator has no admissible real zeros.

At \(x=0\), \(y=- \frac{16}{3}\), giving \(\left(0,- \frac{16}{3}\right)\).

\[x\to 3^-:\ y\to -\infty,\qquad x\to 3^+:\ y\to \infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

(d)

The range is \((-\infty,-5]\cup[3,\infty)\). A horizontal line is tangent at either endpoint height. At each strict interior height of these two ranges it cuts one branch twice. Therefore exactly one distinct intersection occurs at \(h=-5\) or \(h=3\).

questions.title: The boundary parameter must not be discarded
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{k x + 3 x^{2}}{x + 2}\]

\(k\in\mathbb R\). The displayed denominator always excludes \(x=-2\).

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. Find all real \(k\) for which the curve has no stationary points. Include any exceptional cancellation case.

    [5]

  2. Describe the exceptional member corresponding to equality in your answer to (a).

    [1]

  3. For \(k=10\), find the asymptotes.

    [2]

  4. For \(k=10\), sketch the curve and label its axis intersections.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(k\ge6\)

(b) A punctured line \(y=3x\) with hole \((-2,-6)\).

(c) \(x=-2,\quad y=3 x + 4\)

(d) Sketch with the stated asymptotes, correct one-sided approaches and all intercepts.

(a)

Division and differentiation give

\[f(x)=3x+k-6+\frac{12-2k}{x+2},\qquad f\prime(x)=3-\frac{12-2k}{(x+2)^2}\]

If \(k\lt 6\), the equation \((x+2)^2=(12-2k)/3\) has two admissible roots. If \(k\gt 6\), the derivative is strictly positive. At \(k=6\), cancellation gives \(f(x)=3x\) for \(x\ne-2\) and the derivative is 3, so there is still no stationary point. Therefore the complete answer includes equality: \(k\ge6\).

(b)

For \(k=6\), the graph is \(y=3x\) with \((-2,-6)\) deleted. A missing domain point is not a stationary point and is not a vertical asymptote.

(c)

Polynomial division gives

\[f(x)=3 x + 4 - \frac{8}{x + 2}\]

The numerator is non-zero at each real denominator zero. These are genuine vertical asymptotes: \(x=-2\).

The remainder term tends to zero as \(x\to\pm\infty\). Hence the oblique asymptote is \(y=3 x + 4\).

(d)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=-2,\quad y=3 x + 4\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are \(\left(- \frac{10}{3},0\right),\quad \left(0,0\right)\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=0\), giving \(\left(0,0\right)\).

\[x\to -2^-:\ y\to \infty,\qquad x\to -2^+:\ y\to -\infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{- a x - a + x^{2} + x}{x^{2} + 2 x - 3}\]

\(a\notin\{-3,-1,1\}\).

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. State the asymptotes.

    [2]

  2. Find the point at which the curve meets its horizontal asymptote.

    [2]

  3. Derive a quadratic equation for stationary inputs and determine exactly when stationary points exist.

    [5]

  4. Sketch the two members \(a=2\) and \(a=0\), showing how their branch shapes differ.

    [5]

(a) \(x=-3,\ x=1,\ y=1\)

(b) \((4/(a+1)-1,1)\)

(c) \(-3\lt a\lt -1\ \hbox{or}\ -1\lt a\lt 1\)

(d) No stationary points for a = 2; two for a = 0.

(a)

There is no cancellation for the stated a-values. The poles are \(x=-3,1\) and the horizontal asymptote is \(y=1\).

(b)

Put \(t=x+1\) and \(b=a+1\). Then \(f=t(t-b)/(t^2-4)\). Setting \(f=1\) gives \(bt=4\), so the crossing is

\[\left(\frac4{a+1}-1,1\right)\]

The excluded values \(a=-3,-1,1\) ensure that this calculation neither divides by zero nor produces a pole.

(c)

\[\frac{df}{dt}=\frac{bt^2-8t+4b}{(t^2-4)^2}\]

The stationary equation has discriminant \(64-16b^2\). Since \(b\ne0\), there are two distinct stationary inputs precisely when \(-2\lt b\lt 2\). The excluded boundary cases correspond to cancellation at a pole. Thus

\[-3\lt a\lt -1\quad\hbox{or}\quad-1\lt a\lt 1\]

(d)

For \(a=2\), there are no stationary points. For \(a=0\), there are two. Their exact positions and one-sided behaviour follow below.

a = 2

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=-3,\quad x=1,\quad y=1\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are \(\left(-1,0\right),\quad \left(2,0\right)\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=\frac{2}{3}\), giving \(\left(0,\frac{2}{3}\right)\).

The curve meets its horizontal asymptote at \(\left(\frac{1}{3},1\right)\). This crossing is allowed; an asymptote need not be an unattained height.

\[x\to -3^-:\ y\to \infty,\qquad x\to -3^+:\ y\to -\infty\]
\[x\to 1^-:\ y\to \infty,\qquad x\to 1^+:\ y\to -\infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

a = 0

Differentiating and simplifying gives

\[f'(x)=\frac{x^{2} - 6 x - 3}{\left(x - 1\right)^{2} \left(x + 3\right)^{2}}\]

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[x^{2} - 6 x - 3=0\]

The admissible solutions are \(x=3 - 2 \sqrt{3},\quad x=3 + 2 \sqrt{3}\). Substitution into \(f\) gives:

  • \(\left(3 - 2 \sqrt{3},\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)\) — local maximum.
  • \(\left(3 + 2 \sqrt{3},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\right)\) — local minimum.

The classifications follow from the sign change of \(f'(x)\) (or the sign of \(f''(x)\)) at each point.

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=-3,\quad x=1,\quad y=1\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are \(\left(-1,0\right),\quad \left(0,0\right)\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=0\), giving \(\left(0,0\right)\).

The curve meets its horizontal asymptote at \(\left(3,1\right)\). This crossing is allowed; an asymptote need not be an unattained height.

\[x\to -3^-:\ y\to \infty,\qquad x\to -3^+:\ y\to -\infty\]

questions.title: Exactly two intersections in a positive-parameter family
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{3 a + x^{2}}{a + x}\]

\(a\gt 0\).

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. Find the asymptotes.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact stationary x-coordinates and identify the two types of stationary point.

    [3]

  3. Sketch the original curve, showing its intercepts.

    [2]

  4. Sketch the modulus graph.

    [2]

  5. Determine all \(a\gt 0\) for which \(|f(x)|=a\) has exactly two distinct real solutions.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(x=-a,\ y=x-a\)

(b) \(x=-a\pm\sqrt{a(a+3)}\)

(c) Only y-intercept \((0,3)\).

(d) Reflect the entire negative left branch.

(e) \(a\gt 12/5\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f(x)=x-a+\frac{a(a+3)}{x+a}\]

Since \(a\gt 0\), the asymptotes are \(x=-a\) and \(y=x-a\).

(b)

\[f\prime(x)=1-\frac{a(a+3)}{(x+a)^2}\]

Thus the stationary inputs are \(x=-a\pm\sqrt{a(a+3)}\), with heights \(-2a\pm2\sqrt{a(a+3)}\). The left point is a maximum and the right point a minimum.

(c)

The numerator is strictly positive, so there are no x-intercepts. The y-intercept is \((0,3)\). The left branch is negative and the right branch positive.

(d)

Reflect the negative left branch. The two branch minima are the absolute values of their original extremal heights.

(e)

Both signs must be examined. The equation \(f(x)=a\) gives

\[x^2-ax+3a-a^2=0,\qquad\Delta_+=5a^2-12a=a(5a-12)\]

The equation \(f(x)=-a\) gives

\[x^2+ax+3a+a^2=0,\qquad\Delta_-=-3a^2-12a\lt 0\]

Thus the negative-level equation never contributes a real solution. The positive-level equation has exactly two distinct real roots when \(a\gt 12/5\). The pole cannot solve it because substitution of \(x=-a\) gives \(a(a+3)\gt 0\). At \(a=12/5\) there is only one distinct solution.

questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

(a) \(x=1,\quad y=2 x - 1\)

(b) \(\left(1 - \sqrt{2},1 - 4 \sqrt{2}\right)\) (maximum); \(\left(1 + \sqrt{2},1 + 4 \sqrt{2}\right)\) (minimum).

(c) \(y\in \left(-\infty, 1 - 4 \sqrt{2}\right] \cup \left[1 + 4 \sqrt{2}, \infty\right)\).

(d) Sketch with the stated asymptotes, correct one-sided approaches and all intercepts.

(e) \(k=1+4\sqrt2\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Polynomial division gives

\[f(x)=2 x - 1 + \frac{4}{x - 1}\]

The numerator is non-zero at each real denominator zero. These are genuine vertical asymptotes: \(x=1\).

The remainder term tends to zero as \(x\to\pm\infty\). Hence the oblique asymptote is \(y=2 x - 1\).

(b)

Differentiating and simplifying gives

\[f'(x)=\frac{2 \left(x^{2} - 2 x - 1\right)}{\left(x - 1\right)^{2}}\]

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[2 \left(x^{2} - 2 x - 1\right)=0\]

The admissible solutions are \(x=1 - \sqrt{2},\quad x=1 + \sqrt{2}\). Substitution into \(f\) gives:

  • \(\left(1 - \sqrt{2},1 - 4 \sqrt{2}\right)\) — local maximum.
  • \(\left(1 + \sqrt{2},1 + 4 \sqrt{2}\right)\) — local minimum.

The classifications follow from the sign change of \(f'(x)\) (or the sign of \(f''(x)\)) at each point.

(c)

Treat the curve equation as an equation for a real \(x\) at a prescribed height \(y\):

\[- 2 x^{2} + x \left(y + 3\right) - y - 5=0\]

When the quadratic coefficient is non-zero, real roots require

\[\Delta=y^{2} - 2 y - 31\ge0\]

Solving this inequality gives the possible height intervals. Values at which the quadratic coefficient vanishes must be checked in the original equation.

No root of this equation can be a pole, because the numerator and denominator have no common zero. The attainable endpoint heights are included. Therefore the exact range is

\[y\in \left(-\infty, 1 - 4 \sqrt{2}\right] \cup \left[1 + 4 \sqrt{2}, \infty\right)\]

(d)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=1,\quad y=2 x - 1\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are absent: the numerator has no admissible real zeros.

At \(x=0\), \(y=-5\), giving \(\left(0,-5\right)\).

\[x\to 1^-:\ y\to -\infty,\qquad x\to 1^+:\ y\to \infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

(e)

The original range is \((-\infty,1-4\sqrt2]\cup[1+4\sqrt2,\infty)\). On taking absolute values, the two branch minima are \(4\sqrt2-1\) and \(4\sqrt2+1\). At the higher of these two levels, one branch is tangent and the other is cut twice, producing three distinct solutions.

(a)

Polynomial division gives

\[f(x)=2 + \frac{3}{x^{2} + 3}\]

The denominator has no real zeros, so there are no vertical asymptotes.

The remainder term tends to zero as \(x\to\pm\infty\). Hence the horizontal asymptote is \(y=2\).

(b)

Treat the curve equation as an equation for a real \(x\) at a prescribed height \(y\):

\[x^{2} \left(y - 2\right) + 3 y - 9=0\]

When the quadratic coefficient is non-zero, real roots require

\[\Delta=- 12 \left(y - 3\right) \left(y - 2\right)\ge0\]

Solving this inequality gives the possible height intervals. Values at which the quadratic coefficient vanishes must be checked in the original equation.

At \(y=2\), the reduced equation is inconsistent, so this height is not attained.

No root of this equation can be a pole, because the numerator and denominator have no common zero. The attainable endpoint heights are included. Therefore the exact range is

\[y\in \left(2, 3\right]\]

(c)

Differentiating and simplifying gives

\[f'(x)=- \frac{6 x}{\left(x^{2} + 3\right)^{2}}\]

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[- 6 x=0\]

The admissible solutions are \(x=0\). Substitution into \(f\) gives:

  • \(\left(0,3\right)\) — local maximum.

The classifications follow from the sign change of \(f'(x)\) (or the sign of \(f''(x)\)) at each point.

(d)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(y=2\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are absent: the numerator has no admissible real zeros.

At \(x=0\), \(y=3\), giving \(\left(0,3\right)\).

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

(e)

By definition, \(g(x)=1/f(x)\) requires both \(f(x)\) to be defined and \(f(x)\ne0\). Therefore

\[g(x)=\frac{x^{2} + 3}{2 x^{2} + 9},\qquad x\notin \emptyset\]

The simplified expression must not silently enlarge this domain. At each original pole of \(f\), the graph of \(g\) has an open point at height zero, not an included intercept.

\[g'(x)=\frac{6 x}{\left(2 x^{2} + 9\right)^{2}}\]

\(\left(0,\frac{1}{3}\right)\) is a local minimum.

The asymptotes of the simplified expression are \(y=\frac{1}{2}\). Open points are shown explicitly in the sketch.

Since \(2\lt f(x)\le3\) and f is positive, taking reciprocals reverses the bounds: \(1/3\le g(x)\lt 1/2\).

(f)

The denominator \(2x^2+9\) is positive, so multiplying preserves the inequality:

\[5(x^2+3)\lt 2(2x^2+9)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^2\lt 3\]

(b)

Differentiating and simplifying gives

\[f'(x)=\frac{\left(x - 7\right) \left(3 x - 1\right)}{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} \left(x + 3\right)^{2}}\]

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[\left(x - 7\right) \left(3 x - 1\right)=0\]

The admissible solutions are \(x=\frac{1}{3},\quad x=7\). Substitution into \(f\) gives:

  • \(\left(\frac{1}{3},- \frac{4}{5}\right)\) — local maximum.
  • \(\left(7,\frac{4}{5}\right)\) — local minimum.

The classifications follow from the sign change of \(f'(x)\) (or the sign of \(f''(x)\)) at each point.

(c)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=-3,\quad x=2,\quad y=1\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are absent: the numerator has no admissible real zeros.

At \(x=0\), \(y=- \frac{5}{6}\), giving \(\left(0,- \frac{5}{6}\right)\).

The curve meets its horizontal asymptote at \(\left(\frac{11}{3},1\right)\). This crossing is allowed; an asymptote need not be an unattained height.

\[x\to -3^-:\ y\to \infty,\qquad x\to -3^+:\ y\to -\infty\]
\[x\to 2^-:\ y\to -\infty,\qquad x\to 2^+:\ y\to \infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

(d)

By definition, \(g(x)=1/f(x)\) requires both \(f(x)\) to be defined and \(f(x)\ne0\). Therefore

\[g(x)=\frac{x^{2} + x - 6}{x^{2} - 2 x + 5},\qquad x\notin \left\{-3, 2\right\}\]

The simplified expression must not silently enlarge this domain. At each original pole of \(f\), the graph of \(g\) has an open point at height zero, not an included intercept.

\[g'(x)=- \frac{\left(x - 7\right) \left(3 x - 1\right)}{\left(x^{2} - 2 x + 5\right)^{2}}\]

\(\left(\frac{1}{3},- \frac{5}{4}\right)\) is a local minimum.

\(\left(7,\frac{5}{4}\right)\) is a local maximum.

The asymptotes of the simplified expression are \(y=1\). Open points are shown explicitly in the sketch.

(e)

Work on the common domain of \(f\) and \(1/f\). Subtract the right side:

\[\frac1{f(x)}-f(x)=\frac{\left(x - 1\right) \left(2 x + 1\right) \left(3 x - 11\right)}{\left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 3\right) \left(x^{2} - 2 x + 5\right)}\]

Equality occurs at \(f(x)=1\) or \(f(x)=-1\). All original poles and all zeros of \(f\) must also be included as breaks in the sign chart.

questions.title: An isolated point survives the square-root relation
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{x^{2} + 4 x + 4}{x - 1}\]

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. Determine every straight-line asymptote of \(C\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact coordinates of all stationary points and identify their nature.

    [3]

  3. Sketch \(C\), labelling the asymptotes and all intersections with the coordinate axes.

    [3]

  4. On one diagram compare \(y=|f(x)|\) with \(y^2=f(x)\). Give the real x-domain of the second relation and mark any isolated real point.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(x=1,\quad y=x + 5\)

(b) \(\left(-2,0\right)\) (maximum); \(\left(4,12\right)\) (minimum).

(c) Sketch with the stated asymptotes, correct one-sided approaches and all intercepts.

(d) Real x-domain \(\left\{-2\right\} \cup \left(1, \infty\right)\). Stationary points \(\left(4,2 \sqrt{3}\right),\quad \left(4,- 2 \sqrt{3}\right)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Polynomial division gives

\[f(x)=x + 5 + \frac{9}{x - 1}\]

The numerator is non-zero at each real denominator zero. These are genuine vertical asymptotes: \(x=1\).

The remainder term tends to zero as \(x\to\pm\infty\). Hence the oblique asymptote is \(y=x + 5\).

(b)

Differentiating and simplifying gives

\[f'(x)=\frac{\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 2\right)}{\left(x - 1\right)^{2}}\]

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 2\right)=0\]

The admissible solutions are \(x=-2,\quad x=4\). Substitution into \(f\) gives:

  • \(\left(-2,0\right)\) — local maximum.
  • \(\left(4,12\right)\) — local minimum.

The classifications follow from the sign change of \(f'(x)\) (or the sign of \(f''(x)\)) at each point.

(c)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=1,\quad y=x + 5\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are \(\left(-2,0\right)\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=-4\), giving \(\left(0,-4\right)\).

\[x\to 1^-:\ y\to -\infty,\qquad x\to 1^+:\ y\to \infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

(d)

For \(y=|f(x)|\), reflect the entire negative branch (the side \(x\lt 1\)) in the x-axis. The point \((-2,0)\) remains a smooth zero of that modulus graph.

Real ordinates exist only where \(f(x)\ge0\). A sign chart gives

\[x\in \left\{-2\right\} \cup \left(1, \infty\right)\]

On these inputs, draw both \(y=\sqrt{f(x)}\) and \(y=-\sqrt{f(x)}\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are \(\left(-2,0\right)\).

At a non-zero ordinate, implicit differentiation gives \(2y\frac{dy}{dx}=f\prime(x)\). Hence the horizontal-tangent stationary points are \(\left(4,2 \sqrt{3}\right),\quad \left(4,- 2 \sqrt{3}\right)\).

The points \(\left(-2,0\right)\) are isolated real points. They must be shown, but they are not stationary points of a local real branch.
questions.hint_html: An isolated zero with f(x) negative on both sides is still a real point of y² = f(x). It is not a stationary point of a real branch.

questions.title: A bounded curve with no vertical asymptotes
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{x^{2} + 4 x - 2}{x^{2} + 1}\]

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. Determine every straight-line asymptote of \(C\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact coordinates of all stationary points and identify their nature.

    [3]

  3. Sketch \(C\), labelling the asymptotes and all intersections with the coordinate axes.

    [3]

  4. On a separate diagram, sketch \(y=|f(x)|\).

    [2]

  5. Find all levels \(k\) for which \(|f(x)|=k\) has four distinct real solutions.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(y=1\)

(b) \(\left(- \frac{1}{2},-3\right)\) (minimum); \(\left(2,2\right)\) (maximum).

(c) Sketch with the stated asymptotes, correct one-sided approaches and all intercepts.

(d) Reflect precisely the negative portions of the original graph; retain every excluded x-value.

(e) \(k\in(0,1)\cup(1,2)\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Polynomial division gives

\[f(x)=\frac{4 x - 3}{x^{2} + 1} + 1\]

The denominator has no real zeros, so there are no vertical asymptotes.

The remainder term tends to zero as \(x\to\pm\infty\). Hence the horizontal asymptote is \(y=1\).

(b)

Differentiating and simplifying gives

\[f'(x)=- \frac{2 \left(x - 2\right) \left(2 x + 1\right)}{\left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}}\]

The denominator of the original function must remain non-zero. Thus stationary points come from

\[- 2 \left(x - 2\right) \left(2 x + 1\right)=0\]

The admissible solutions are \(x=- \frac{1}{2},\quad x=2\). Substitution into \(f\) gives:

  • \(\left(- \frac{1}{2},-3\right)\) — local minimum.
  • \(\left(2,2\right)\) — local maximum.

The classifications follow from the sign change of \(f'(x)\) (or the sign of \(f''(x)\)) at each point.

(c)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(y=1\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are \(\left(- \sqrt{6} - 2,0\right),\quad \left(-2 + \sqrt{6},0\right)\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=-2\), giving \(\left(0,-2\right)\).

The curve meets its horizontal asymptote at \(\left(\frac{3}{4},1\right)\). This crossing is allowed; an asymptote need not be an unattained height.

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

(d)

Keep points with \(f(x)\ge0\) fixed and reflect the portions with \(f(x)\lt0\) in the \(x\)-axis. The domain is unchanged.

The zeros remain at \(x=- \sqrt{6} - 2,\quad x=-2 + \sqrt{6}\). A simple zero generally becomes a corner; a repeated zero can remain smooth.

At each genuine vertical asymptote the reflected graph tends to \(+\infty\) on both sides. For large positive and negative \(x\), take the absolute value of the corresponding asymptotic height.

(e)

The original range is \([-3,2]\), with extrema at \((-1/2,-3)\) and \((2,2)\). For \(0\lt k\lt 2\), the levels \(k\) and \(-k\) each normally have two preimages. At \(k=1\), however, the positive level is the horizontal-asymptote height and \(f(x)=1\) reduces to \(4x-3=0\), with only one solution. At \(k=2\) there are three distinct solutions because of tangency; for larger k there cannot be four.

\[k\in(0,1)\cup(1,2)\]

questions.title: An unattained infimum determines the boundary case
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{x - 2}\]

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. Determine every straight-line asymptote of \(C\).

    [3]

  2. Determine the exact range of \(f\), using an equation in \(x\) and a discriminant. Justify every included or excluded endpoint.

    [4]

  3. Sketch \(C\), labelling the asymptotes and all intersections with the coordinate axes.

    [2]

  4. On one diagram sketch \(y=|f(x)|\) and \(y=|x|-2\), stating their axis intersections.

    [2]

  5. Find all real \(c\) for which \(|f(x)|\le|x|+c\) has no real solution. Justify the boundary value.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(x=2,\quad y=x + 2\)

(b) \(y\in \left(-\infty, 0\right] \cup \left[8, \infty\right)\).

(c) Sketch with the stated asymptotes, correct one-sided approaches and all intercepts.

(d) Intercepts: \((0,0)\) for |f|; \((0,-2),(\pm2,0)\) for |x|−2.

(e) \(c\le-2\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Polynomial division gives

\[f(x)=x + 2 + \frac{4}{x - 2}\]

The numerator is non-zero at each real denominator zero. These are genuine vertical asymptotes: \(x=2\).

The remainder term tends to zero as \(x\to\pm\infty\). Hence the oblique asymptote is \(y=x + 2\).

(b)

Treat the curve equation as an equation for a real \(x\) at a prescribed height \(y\):

\[- x^{2} + x y - 2 y=0\]

When the quadratic coefficient is non-zero, real roots require

\[\Delta=y \left(y - 8\right)\ge0\]

Solving this inequality gives the possible height intervals. Values at which the quadratic coefficient vanishes must be checked in the original equation.

No root of this equation can be a pole, because the numerator and denominator have no common zero. The attainable endpoint heights are included. Therefore the exact range is

\[y\in \left(-\infty, 0\right] \cup \left[8, \infty\right)\]

(c)

The straight-line asymptotes are \(x=2,\quad y=x + 2\).

The \(x\)-axis intersections are \(\left(0,0\right)\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=0\), giving \(\left(0,0\right)\).

\[x\to 2^-:\ y\to -\infty,\qquad x\to 2^+:\ y\to \infty\]

Use the derivative sign and the stationary points to connect the branches. Never join a curve across a vertical asymptote. Dashed lines in the graph denote asymptotes.

(d)

The comparison graph \(y=|x|-2\) has vertex \((0,-2)\) and zeros at \((-2,0)\) and \((2,0)\). The modulus curve has only the intercept \((0,0)\) and is undefined at x = 2.

(e)

Put \(H(x)=|f(x)|-|x|\). For \(x\lt 0\),

\[H(x)=\frac{x^2}{2-x}+x=-2+\frac4{2-x}\gt -2\]

As \(x\to-\infty\), this approaches −2 but never equals −2. If \(0\le x\lt 2\), then \(|f(x)|\ge0\gt x-2\). If \(x\gt 2\),

\[H(x)=\frac{x^2}{x-2}-x=2+\frac4{x-2}\gt 2\]

Thus \(H(x)\gt -2\) everywhere on the domain, and its infimum is −2, not attained. For every \(c\gt -2\), sufficiently negative x gives \(H(x)\le c\). Therefore the inequality has no solution exactly when \(c\le-2\).
questions.hint_html: Study H(x) = |f(x)| − |x|. Distinguish a minimum that is attained from an infimum approached only as x tends to infinity.

questions.title: Two curves with a common pole but no intersections
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is given by \(y=f(x)\), where

\[f(x)=\frac{a x - a}{x + 3}\]

\(a\gt 4\).

Unless a part states otherwise, use the natural real domain of the displayed function and give exact answers.

  1. The first curve \(C_1\) has equation \(y=f(x)\). State its asymptotes.

    [2]

  2. The second curve \(C_2\) is given by \(y=g(x)=\frac{a x + 3 a + x^{2} + 6 x + 13}{x + 3}\). Find its oblique asymptote.

    [2]

  3. Prove that the two curves do not intersect and identify which is higher on each side of their common pole.

    [2]

  4. Find and classify the stationary points of \(C_2\).

    [3]

  5. Sketch both curves on one set of axes. You need not find the x-intercepts of \(C_2\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(x=-3,\ y=a\)

(b) \(y=x+a+3\)

(c) No intersections; C₂ is higher for x > −3 and lower for x < −3.

(d) \((-5,a-4),\ (-1,a+4)\)

(e) Use the two asymptotes at infinity, the common pole and the proven ordering.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(f(x)=a-4a/(x+3)\). Hence the asymptotes of \(C_1\) are \(x=-3\) and \(y=a\).

(b)

\[g(x)=x+a+3+\frac4{x+3}\]

Thus the oblique asymptote of \(C_2\) is \(y=x+a+3\); its vertical asymptote is also \(x=-3\).

(c)

\[g(x)-f(x)=\frac{(x+3)^2+4a+4}{x+3}\]

The numerator is strictly positive for \(a\gt 4\). It cannot be zero, so the curves do not intersect. Moreover \(g\gt f\) to the right of the common pole and \(g\lt f\) to the left.

(d)

\[g\prime(x)=1-\frac4{(x+3)^2}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=-5,-1\]

The stationary points of \(C_2\) are \((-5,a-4)\) (maximum) and \((-1,a+4)\) (minimum).

(e)

For \(C_1\), the intercepts are \((1,0)\) and \((0,-a/3)\). It approaches positive infinity at the pole from the left and negative infinity from the right. For \(C_2\), these directions are reversed. Use the ordering proved in (c), so the curves never cross.
questions.hint_html: Subtract the two functions over their common denominator. Completing the square in the numerator proves non-intersection and determines their ordering.
